utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. Prosecution today is Mr. Thayer and Mr. Vanderpuye. And Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic. All right. I think we can start. The witness is here. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome. Ms. Fauveau will be concluding her examination-in-chief and then we see where we go from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D954. This is a report, a logistic report of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina about Srebrenica on the 25th of May, 1994, which indicates the coming of food for the brigade of the GO Srebrenica. Could page 2 in B/C/S be displayed, please, and for English it's at the end of page 1, at the bottom of page 1. Could we see page 2 in B/C/S, please, at the bottom of the page. At the bottom of this chart where you can see the food stuffs which the 8th group of Srebrenica obtained, one can see that all the items, food stuffs, were coming from the humanitarian aid and supplied by [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What are the possible consequences when an army uses humanitarian aid? What are the possible consequences when this aid goes to the territory of the other party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an operative document of the 28th Division. It shows the situation regarding the food supplies, the quantities as shown, as well as how many days they were expected to last. You can see that the only source of supplies for the 28th Division was in fact humanitarian aid. This is something that the Army Republika Srpska knew, they knew that the 28th Divisions only logistical assistance was coming through humanitarian aid. This fact also indicates that humanitarian aid quantities were being closely monitored in terms of the population. The citizens who were the real addressees of this humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1351. And more specifically, page 7 in the B/C/S text and page 13 and 14 for the English text. Excuse me, the page just before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see item 9.4. This item mentioned tasks for the administration for logistics of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and under 9.4 we can see that the coordination and cooperation with international humanitarian organisations in order to secure medicines and medical stuff and food for the needs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The cooperation of international humanitarian organisations with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it have an effect on the relations of the Army of the Republika Srpska towards humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly true that the cooperation of various humanitarian organisations with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina looked very much like actual logistical assistance being provided to the army. It was significantly affecting the reservations expressed by Republika Srpska and the Army Republika Srpska about the real humanitarian objectives of these organisations. If we look at item 9.4, that talks about international humanitarian organisations and their coordination in terms of securing logistical support for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I would like to say is that item or paragraph 9.1 also indicates this in a certain way because 9.1 talks about the distribution of mines and explosives, and we all know that at the time there was a blockade on and no weapons, mines, or explosives were coming through to that particular sector of the front. This is also about the various aspects of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D777. It's a document from the Army of Republika Srpska of the 18th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of the page you can see a paragraph in which the staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska informs its subordinate units about the activities and intelligence, intelligence activities, in which certain members of the UNHCR were acting. The fact of having such information, did it have any influence on the authorisation of passage granted to convoys, for convoys? Did this fact have an influence on the authorisations? Did this fact -- could this fact have an influence on the authorisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The fact that humanitarian aid was being misused, or rather, used to revitalise and resupply the enemy could have led to it slowing down or stopping humanitarian aid all together until such time as it could be checked. If we look at this document, we see that a distribution of supplies was allowed but not ordered. There was an order to step up control and this was necessary. Units of the Army of Republika Srpska were warned about the fact that their behaviour towards members of these international humanitarian organisations are to be dignified instead of arrogant, which tell us about their general attitude to humanitarian aid. And there was also a specific caution that was issued to the effect that the reporting itself had to be more detailed and more careful in terms of how humanitarian aid was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1362. This comes from the 28th Division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the army, of the 26th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at the last paragraph which shows that the translator who was working for Medecins Sans Frontieres at Srebrenica communicated to the intelligence office of the 28th Division in Srebrenica certain informations. Does the activity of the interpreter of Medecins Sans Frontieres at Srebrenica confirm the activities of intelligence of certain members of the humanitarian organisations, international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activities of this interpreter would seem to indicate that the international humanitarian organisations were being misused or used for the purposes of intelligence of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These activities were carefully planned and they were aimed at specific goals. It is by no means an error that this was recorded here. It wasn't meant to lead to confusion. This was meant to obtain information. This system was functioning and it was carefully laid out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to not place his hand in front of his mouth when he gives his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General. General, when you are giving your answers sometimes you put your hands in front of your mouth. This is interrupting the flow of your words in the direction of the microphone and the interpreters are having problems, so if you could kindly remove your hands from in front of your mouth when you talk. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally I would like the witness be shown two documents concerning the activities of members of UNPROFOR. The first is 5D1367. This is a document from the security service, State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Gorazde, dated 17 June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please read this document, which is rather brief, and then I'll show you the next document to ask you a question concerning both documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document 5D1369.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is your conclusion concerning the activities of members of UNPROFOR which are described in these two documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two documents indicate that there was a system of intelligence exchanged between UNPROFOR and the BH Army. The simplest method of cooperation between intelligence bodies is forwarding information. Forwarding unprocessed information, specifically. One can see that this system of exchange or cooperation was perfected. This is not just about forwarding or submitting information. This is also about checking information and this is key when you are trying to verify a piece of information. They are here checking information through the contact with Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- on the other hand, there was the channel that was designed from the most high ranking officers of the UNPROFOR, General Sweet [phoen] in this case, having a reliable access to the other side in disguise as it were. One can see that the UNPROFOR people knew very well what the situation was in Srebrenica, and this confirms what I said in my expert report that the situation was closely monitored and well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What consequences and what activities of the members of the UNPROFOR could have had on the members of the UNPROFOR and Republika Srpska? Which consequences this behaviour could have had on the relations between the UNPROFOR and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of behaviour could easily have led to a total communications breakdown or overall communications to be checked. Nevertheless, when one looks at all these documents, the Army of Republika Srpska was merely stepping up control. Sometimes they would send protest notes just to make public the fact that they were perfectly aware of what was being done and who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Fauveau. Now, let's go make the round. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, I represent Vujadin Popovic. I will ask you a couple of questions about your evidence. Among other things, on day one of your testimony you told us about Directive number 4. You said that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was using civilians as a shield or, rather, as a component of their armed forces. I would like to kindly ask you to please elaborate on that. What does it mean to use one's own civilian population as a component in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too, first of all. I addressed this problem on several occasions in varying situations throughout my evidence, throughout the presentation of my expert reports before this Tribunal. I will try to tackle this as a whole now since it wasn't tackled as a whole necessarily by my expert report. It is generally known and everybody in the BH Army knew well, especially the leading officers who went way back to the JNA, about the Geneva Conventions and the rules of war, they knew about how civilians were to be treated. They also knew that on the other side, the members of the Army Republika Srpska also knew about how civilians were to be treated. They permanently and consistently misused the following activities. Sometimes they would dress up as civilians and operate as soldiers. They often dressed up as women civilians again but with a peculiar status, a status that was a status apart, and they were using this in order to preform operations. And they would keep their own people, the population close by at all times, knowing that this was a different kind of target and that they were not likely to be targeted in the same way as soldiers. They organised their commands in civilian homes as well as other elements of their units combat structure. They used company premises to house certain elements of their armed forces. Even outside Srebrenica, especially in other areas, as was generally well known, they used civilian facilities and facilities belonging to the health system to install their fire-power or certain positions for which they were monitoring the situation. The fact remains that when you use a civilian facility in order to preform military operations to establish your command or use it for any military purpose whatsoever, you are turning the civilian facility into a military facility thereby violating these very fundamental rules of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just in order to be perfectly clear about this, what you have just been telling us about, does this apply throughout the existence of the enclaves all the way up until July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applies to the entire period from the beginning to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you another question. Given the fact that Srebrenica was declared a protected area, what about its status itself as a protected area, was this something that was used during the war by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, of all things, is one of the segments that came under scrutiny in my expert report. I tried to be as specific and precise as I could about this. There were a number of prerequisites for the area to be declared a protected area but only the first prerequisite was ever met and a decision was taken accordingly. There were a number of other conditions that were to be put into place. For example, defining the area in more specific terms. But this was constantly being obstructed by the BH Army and they were receiving assistance from UNPROFOR in this. In order to have mobilisation, false reports were being sent all the time that there had been a demilitarisation throughout the area although there was a well-armed operative group still inside. In order to make sure there was appropriate control, there was a lot of obstruction going on, even if we know that helicopters were used and also across the grounds military equipment was being brought in as well as various forms of military logistics by the 28th Division and previously by the operations group. In order to inform all the parties in this conflict about all the important aspects, there was obstruction going on. For example, there is a protest note about firing from within the enclave but you can't see the protest note when a unit was leaving. All of this indicates that no demilitarisation had been carried out and that in actual fact this was no protected area whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about this protest note because there was firing coming from within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please just look at a document that we already looked at yesterday. This is P1349.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is, this document was sent by the DutchBat commander to the president of the Srebrenica municipality complaining because the Muslim forces from within the enclave had been firing, which they were not allowed to do under the provisions of the agreement on the establishment of a safe area. However, there was something else that I wanted to ask you. Among other things paragraph 2 of this document says that eight bullets were fired from small arms from somewhere near the post office building. We do know for a fact that the post office building was in the immediate vicinity of the hospital. So I would like to ask you this: From your perspective as an expert, what do you think about this situation? One of the parties in conflict opens fire from a weapon that is mounted near a building like this, a building that should be safe from all form of combat operations, how does that strike you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question both calls for speculation and also mischaracterizes the evidence. There's no statement in this document that says that the weapon was mounted where Mr. Zivanovic has indicated. It says that it was fired from near that location but there's no indication other than that. So I would appreciate if my colleague could rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document indicates that the fire was opened from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Near the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- the building PTT building, and we know from our visit to the Srebrenica that it is very near to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less we are fine with the question. So General, if you can answer it, please go ahead. But one moment, because my recollection also is that the PTT is on one side of the street and the hospital is on the other side of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but very near.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to make that clear. And between one and the other, I reckon there is a distance of about 200 metres roughly because the hospital, then you have to go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's a rough guess, it's a rough guess, and I went there twice already, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document speaks of several points, not only the one we have been discussing. First of all, the protest is addressed to the president of Srebrenica municipality in spite of the fact that it has been proved beyond doubt that the battalion commander knew that in Srebrenica there was the command of the 28th Division. And this was a time when the 28th Division was reformed. He knew that the 28th Division was not subordinated to the president of the municipality, but to the command of the 2nd Corps. So this warning creates the illusion that in the municipality there was the civilian population and somebody was firing at them. On the other hand, the very fact that information arrived that firing was coming from the vicinity of the post office, this doesn't mean that this could not have been used in any other way. For example, any other hospital. The fact is that in the town when there were two civilian facilities, the post office and the hospital, and fire was being opened from there so that is the reason for the warning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In line 6, somebody was firing, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the fact that in the post office building there was part of the UN staff have anything to do with this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be, but that is not crucial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are speculating here. Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Morning, no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. -- okay, you are correct, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Morning Mr. President, morning Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stephane Bourgon and together with my colleagues present with me here this morning, Ms. Jelena Nikolic and Ms. Marie Claude Fournie, together we represent Dragan Nikolic in these proceedings. General, first if you can confirm that you and I unfortunately did not have the opportunity to meet with a view to discussing your report; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you can confirm that you did meet briefly with my colleague, Mrs. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, this morning I have two types of questions for you, some of which relate directly to your testimony, and then at the end I have a second part of questions where I'm going to try and take advantage of your vast experience as a general and to ask you for your opinion with some practical situations. If at any time there are questions you do not understand, please do not hesitate to ask me to repeat my questions. The first topic I would like to address is the presence of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. In your report at paragraph 17, you mentioned the presence in Srebrenica and Potocari of a number of units which together make up the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I take it you are familiar with the units that make up the 28th Division who were present there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with their organisation and functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, at paragraphs 164 to 182 of your report, you refer to the breakout from encirclement by the 28th Division. And more particularly, at paragraph 161, you mention two things. Firstly, that the 28th Division which was not fully used in the Srebrenica enclave was necessary or even essential for the BiH Army for future and final operations. Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the second thing you mentioned in the same paragraph is that the breakout from encirclement was carried out on orders from the Superior Command of the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following: Bearing in mind what you have in your report and on the basis of your military expertise and all the documents you've reviewed to prepare your expert report, in your opinion, did the 28th Division leave the Srebrenica enclave voluntarily or was it forced out by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand your question, and I consider it necessary before replying to draw attention to a point which I feel has been misunderstood by many participants. If I'm wrong, I apologise, but that's my impression. I think it has not been fully understood what reforming of the 8th Operative Group and making it -- transforming it into the 28th Division means. That's why I will state that very briefly. The reforming of the 8th Operative Group, which was an operative unit, and as such was a large and complicated unit for operations in that area, and in some instances it behaved like an elephant in a china shop, this all represented the preparation of the BH Army for fast and efficient action; that is, breakout from encirclement. The 28th Division prepared carefully for the breakout from encirclement starting from February and March 1995 by stepping up terrorist activities, and, in a measured way, stepping up these terrorist activities so as to provoke the separation of the Srebrenica and Zepa areas. And when they set out to separate them, they actually withdrew and then set out to break out from encirclement, and thus surprised the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted]. So my final answer is, they did not leave -- the reason they left was to trick the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted] and to break out from the encirclement successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And that additional information is indeed very useful. Another issue you touch upon during your examination-in-chief concerns the strategic objectives of the Republika Srpska in relation to the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. And my question is the following: On the basis of your military knowledge and all the documents you reviewed, did you perceive any indication of the existence of a plan or policy, whether at the state level or the VRS level, to destroy the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war I have not found any indication of such a plan in any document. No such plan existed either in Srebrenica or for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd just like to come back to page 15, line 12. Apparently there was a mistake. It should read "thus surprised the VRS" and not surprised the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm looking at it. In my mind I was letting you finish because it's obvious that there is a mistake here. It occurs twice actually, it's on line 15 of page 15, and in lines 13, and I thought I saw it. 13 and 15 anyway, where we see "Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," it should be the "VRS."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, let's continue with our questions. The next -- another topic you discussed during your examination-in-chief is the difference between superior officers and subordinate officers, as well as between senior or junior officers. And that was at page 29980 and 29981 on 12th of January. That was on Monday. Now, more specifically, you provided a criteria which allows to establish that if you have a number of officers present in the same place, which one of them, if they are at the same level in the chain of command, would be the most senior. You recall testifying to that effect, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on this basis, I would like to obtain your opinion as to whom is the senior officer in the following scenario: In this scenario a number of conscripts, non-commissioned officers, and officers, all members of the same brigade are present at the same place. Amongst these persons, you have the assistant commander for security who bears the rank of 2nd lieutenant, and you have the assistant commander for logistics who bears the rank of captain. Who, in your opinion, General, is the senior officer present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this scenario, the most senior officer is the captain who is the assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like now to turn to paragraphs 25 to 34 of your report where you discuss the organisation and the functioning of the VRS. And more specifically, you address the difference between a line staff type of organisation and a line functional type of organisation. And my first question in this regard relates to paragraph 30 of your report, where you say the following: "Analysis of the structure of commands in the VRS and their competences shows that a line staff type of organisation was established in the VRS." General, is this still your opinion today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different topic, General, which is -- has to do with a document which was shown to you during your examination-in-chief, and that is 5D1207.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have this document in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, this document will appear on the screen before you, and I would like to ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have both the English and the B/C/S on the screen, on page 1 for both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, do you remember being asked some questions about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the top part, you can confirm that this document, the sending agency of this document, is the Main Staff of the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking at the second block, you can confirm that this document is being sent to four specific addressees who are mentioned there, and that includes the assistant commander for logistics, the commander of the command of the Drina Corps, the chief of security of the Drina Corps, as well as the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to note a difference between the English version of this document, or the translation in English, and the original in B/C/S, whereas there is no "to." In the English version on the second line, you have "to commander of the command," those words, "to," do not appear in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, can you confirm that this document when you look at a little lower down on the first page that it is being issued on the basis of a previous order issued by the Main Staff on 23 January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like to do at this time is to go to this document which was not shown to you during your examination-in-chief, and that is in e-court, please, 5D1206.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have both the English and the B/C/S version on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, do you see this document, and my first question is can you confirm that this is indeed the document which was referred to in the first one that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once again, this document, as you can see, is sent by the Main Staff, and can you also confirm that it is addressed personally to the commander of all units mentioned at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would also like to note a difference between the English and -- translation and the original B/C/S document, whereas the English version in the top part says "president of the republic" which is not a correct translation. The original version says simply "Republika Srpska" and does not have the word "president."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We heard during your testimony in chief that the object of these two documents related to the preparation, organisation, and carrying out of the briefing on combat readiness of the VRS in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, just to clarify the difference in translation that you pointed out a minute ago. The English version says four things. First mentions the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Then it mentions the president of the republic. Then it mentions strictly confidential number, et cetera. And then it mentions the date. According to my interpretation of what I see in the B/C/S version there are three things only; namely, the entry "president of the republic" should disappear completely. And what you should have is "the Main Staff," "Glavni Stab, Vojska Republika Srpska," which is of the Army of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, this briefing that was about to take place, of course we know from the date January of 1995 that this was taking place during the war, and I think you may have referred to this in your testimony, but of course, can you confirm that this is of the very, very important event where during the war all the senior members of the army of the VRS and the political leadership will be at the same place at one specific time, this can be very dangerous? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my examination-in-chief I said that and I now confirm it. This was the most important event at that time in that area and from the security viewpoint for management of the state and military management, it can be considered the most crucial activity taking place in the whole course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now in the same document in page 3 in the B/C/S version, and page 5 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, I'd like you to look at paragraph 4 of the document that will appear before you. Do you see paragraph 4, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it you would agree that this paragraph 4 assigns a specific task to the logistics sector of VRS Main Staff, and that is to prepare basically the room for the briefing, and to provide the food also; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 5 of the document, this document assigns specific taskings to the security and intelligence sector of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my understanding of paragraph 5 is that by this paragraph, General Tolimir is given the authority to take all necessary measures for the briefings to be carried out without hindrance and also to ensure to protect and secure the participants to this briefing. Would that be a correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So in other words, the authority give be to General Tolimir by this document covers all aspects related to the smooth running of the meeting without being disturbed, but also the safety and protection of all participants?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything you said is correct. If one alludes to the item in the previous order relating to guards, I think that is outside of that aspect, but that is not a problem because it's up to the command to raise the guard duty to a higher level [as interpreted], whereas the other points are all within the purview of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this document that you have before you now, you agree that this is the first one that was issued in respect to taskings given for this briefing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 6 of that document, you also have specific tasks which are given to the -- I just want to use the exact term, to the morale guidance and psychological preparation sector of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, apparently there's a mistake in interpretation on page 22, line 6. Where it says "the guard duty to a higher level" the witness would have said "to the command level." In the meantime if we can move to the last page of this document, please, in both B/C/S and in English. It's the same page in B/C/S, but the English page we have to go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the -- who was the signing authority or the issuing authority for this document, we see that it's the commander himself, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just to make it so that we understand that this is an order by which the commander of the army, Ratko Mladic, gave some specific taskings to some of the generals including General Tolimir at paragraph 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can come back now to the -- this document which was issued after, which is 5D1207. And if I can have page 2 in B/C/S and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, General, if we look at the signature block, we see two things here. First, that whoever signed it appears to have done it for General Tolimir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that General Tolimir in issuing this document, now that you have seen the order issued previously by Mladic, that General Tolimir was merely issuing taskings on the basis of the authority he had been given by Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move, General, to a different series of questions. And as I mentioned at the beginning, these questions relate really to your expertise and vast experience as a general in the VRS. And one of the things you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was a general in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, my mistake. Sorry, General. This question also relates to paragraph 46 of your report where you state that in the VRS, establishments duties are identified either as being single or dual. Do you recall this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that one of the examples of a dual duty is that of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that the duty of the Chief of Staff is dual because if the commander of the unit is absent, then the Chief of Staff must replace them in his capacity as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. But maybe this requires a small additional explanation. Even if a Chief of Staff did not have to be also deputy commander, whenever a commander was away he would still be standing in for him according to all the other criteria being the most senior officer of that particular command, and we discussed the criteria of seniority. When you have this provision that someone is at the same time deputising, what this means in a normal regular situation, when the Chief of Staff is there, then he can stand in for him, even if there is someone who is senior. It is precisely defined who can stand in for the commander and that's why he's also the deputy. Whoever drew up the structure determined ahead of time only this or that person can possibly stand in for the commander when the commander is away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's very useful. I also would like to address quickly paragraph 71 of your report in which you list the eight principles which form the basis of command in the VRS. I take it, General, you are familiar with these eight principles?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the first of these principles which you referred to as being singleness of command, you will agree with me that according to this principle, the commander of a military unit has an indivisible and exclusive right to command all subordinate units in that it is the commander who bears responsibility for the condition, combat readiness, and use of the units as well as for the proper execution of all tasks assigned to the unit, and that is described in paragraphs also of your report at 73. Do you agree that this being singleness of command is what makes the commander and gives to the commander all of this authority and responsibility within a unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. This is the supreme principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in other words, a unit can only have, according to this principle, one commander who is responsible for everything that takes place in his unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like to do now is to ask you on the basis of what was just mentioned about the Chief of Staff standing in for the commander, I'd like to ask for your expert opinion concerning the exercise of command by the Chief of Staff who is acting in his capacity as deputy commander in the absence of the brigade commander. Do you understand the situation I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, suppose the Chief of Staff who holds the rank of major and who is present at the brigade command is facing a critical situation, including a grave shortage of resources and especially of experienced officers, and that this makes it almost impossible for him to accomplish the tasks the brigade has been ordered to perform. On this basis, General, my first question is the following: If the Chief of Staff decides to replace the officer on duty at the brigade forward command post because he needs him for some other purpose, would you expect the Chief of Staff to personally select the officer he will send to the forward command post to replace the officer who is there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just provided a specific example. The Chief of Staff personally stands in for the duty officer. If he takes that type of action that you suggest, given the fact that his brigade is facing a critical situation, his Chief of Staff literally and successfully stands in for the commander in keeping with all the rules. There is one thing that I would like to invoke though, when a superior officer is not present, when it's necessary to take urgent steps or take steps that cannot be postponed, especially emergency situations involving combat and so on and so forth, the most senior commander will take over command and deal with it right there and then. If we have any other type of information, this man will have to first confer with his own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General, that's also very useful, but I'd like maybe to clarify or confirm that you did understand the situation I was referring to. Now we have the Chief of Staff who is standing in because he is acting in the absence of his commander, and one of the things he must do at a certain time is to replace the officer who is at the forward command post of the brigade because he needs him for some purpose. And I suggest to you that when the time comes to replace this officer, because he is facing this critical situation and the shortage of experience officer, that he will select himself who he will send to replace the officer who is presently at the forward command post. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if I could just -- I'm, sorry, if I could just ask my colleague if he could clarify the question a little bit because in the initial part of the question he uses the phrase "Chief of Staff who is standing in because he must do at the time is to replace the officer." My point of concern is, when you are talking about the Chief of Staff standing in, whether or not that is the operative term or whether or not the Chief of Staff is the deputy commander and is acting in that capacity, just so it's clear for the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with my colleague, I will just make that scenario very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, all my questions relate to a situation where it happens in a brigade, the brigade commander is absent, and in his absence the Chief of Staff is exercising command over the brigade. So that's the basis for all my questions. And the specific scenario I was asking you is that in this situation, considering that a situation is very critical and that there's a shortage of officers and especially of experienced officers, the Chief of Staff decides to replace the officer who is presently at the forward command post. And my proposition to you is that when the Chief of Staff does something like that in this scenario, he will of course select carefully who he will send there, especially because he is short of experienced officers. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question fully. I can provide a comment characterizing the situation. I believe that it will be readily intelligible to all. If he needs the officer who happens to be the duty officer, if he has to replace this officer because he needs to use him for some other purpose or task, and this has nothing to go do with any of the other officers, which means that he needs this officer individually to deal with a certain task in situations such as these, normally one says, Replace this man, send him back, and then assign someone else, the next man in line, so to speak. If there is a critical situation and he needs a large number of officers, and that seems to be the situation that you are hypothesising about. In such a situation this man will probably say: Give me this man, have him replaced, and send this other man stand in for him and to act as the duty officer. That is the only situation; if he needs a large number of officer in order to perform a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One last question before the break which relates directly to this situation. Having decided to replace the officer at the forward command post, would you agree with me it would be important for the Chief of Staff to at least warn the brigade duty officer so that at least this change would be recorded in the brigade duty officer notebook or log-book? How important would that be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this officer is at the command post and it's important for it to be recorded that there was a replacement at the command post, and the duty officer in the brigade would later be familiarised with this or informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how important based on all of your military experience, how important is it that the duty officer be informed that there was indeed a change of the duty officer of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes one moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He's already answered the question, Mr. President. I won't go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's time for the break. I have about 15 to 20 minutes at the most which will be well within my hour and a half I'd announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an important witness, we are not restricting anyone. So let's have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have been told Mr. McCloskey would like to address the Chamber. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. And incidentally, my apologies to you. I should have put on the record that soon after we started the sitting this morning you showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just an important scheduling concern. I've been discussing with my team, with Mr. Vanderpuye, and with the Defence, and it appears Mr. Vanderpuye will begin his cross-examination today, and we are hoping he will be done by Monday, at the end of the day. It's possible it could go into Tuesday. And that leaves us with - on the schedule - a one Gvero witness who is scheduled for, I believe, 8 hours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. We had the filing this morning, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The filing was for no February witnesses, but we've got two more weeks of January, I believe we have the Gvero expert scheduled, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Gvero expert -- it doesn't appear it's going to take all next week and certainly the next week of January, so we are just looking for some clarity so we know who to prepare for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know the -- certainly the Pandurevic team is looking for more clarity than I am, I think, since they are up. And I know Mr. Josse is taking this information in as we are giving it to him, and he's -- and he's, you know, working on it, as is Mr. Krgovic. And I gave this information to them before right at the last break, but we really need some clarity before the end of today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- so we know who to prepare for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Yes, Mr. Josse, let's hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's fair to say that we are not very anxious to discuss this particular topic at this particular juncture. We felt obliged to send out that e-mail yesterday because we were aware that everyone needed to know where they stood in relation to February. We are actively considering our position in relation to January really all the time. We, beyond that, we are not very anxious to commit ourselves one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that -- had you said it months ago, but not on the eve at the 11th hour because basically let's put it like this. Mr. Bourgon is almost finished, then there is the cross-examination, your cross-examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for which you had asked three hours. I was going to ask you whether you still need three hours three not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krgovic is going to cross-examine the witness. He thinks he is going to be less time than that, about 2 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And taking the rest, basically it means as Mr. McCloskey put it, that Mr. Vanderpuye will probably be called upon to start his cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a chance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. The Prosecution had asked for 12 hours, which from what Mr. McCloskey said I understand is going to be reduced. If that takes us to Tuesday, to Tuesday, we are literally on the eve. We need to know what is going to happen as soon as Mr. Vanderpuye finishes with -- I don't know if I'm saying something that my colleagues disagree with, but I think at this point in time out of loyalty to the Trial Chamber and also to the -- yourself and the Pandurevic Defence team, I mean, we need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say this, we have done our best over the last few days to liaise closely with the Pandurevic Defence team. That being said, any problems that are occurring are down, I'm certainly not passing Mr. Haynes' direction, they should be directed to me rather than to him. I want to make that clear. I'm not passing the buck in any way at all. I can see and understand the concern of the Trial Chamber. What I would ask for is the next break to have a further discussion with Mr. Krgovic and General Gvero, and we will give a further report at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, I think that's fair enough. Thank you, Mr. Josse. And thank you, Mr. Krgovic, as well. And Mr. McCloskey. So, let's bring the witness, the General back in. What you need to understand is we can't allow ourselves the situation to arise whereby, say on Tuesday we find ourselves in a position where we don't know what is going to happen. Maybe we'll have two days, three days when we cannot sit. I mean, that's a situation which we expect you to help us avoid. Let us keep that in mind. And I'm sure you will because I know very well the tradition, legal tradition you come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, we are going to proceed. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, General. I have about ten more questions to ask you, and they all have to do with the same situation we were discussing before the break, and let me just repeat that so that we know what the basic facts are. This takes place in a brigade. The brigade commander is absent. The Chief of Staff is exercising command over the brigade. The situation is critical, including a grave shortage of resources. In this situation, General, suppose the Chief of Staff is informed by one of the brigade assistant commanders who bears the rank of 2nd lieutenant, that he received information by telephone from an officer from the corps that the brigade must accomplish an additional task which will require the use of resources which will put in danger the safety of the brigade and the ability of the brigade to accomplish it's ongoing activities. Do I need to repeat this, General, or you understand the facts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So my question in this circumstance is, would you expect that before taking any action to accomplish this additional task, the Chief of Staff would first attempt to confirm what the additional tasking really consists of and who is the real authority behind it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific situation that you are asking me about contains two important elements. One, if this is a new situation, an unusual situation or an activity that significantly disrupts the working plan of the unit, or if this is an activity that is not in keeping with what is considered regular activity, it is only to be expected that the Chief of Staff should acquire additional information or he should run additional checks, perform additional checks. If this activity is something that is repeated over time with a certain frequency, then there is no need for any additional checks. Quite simply, it is simply extended, and it is dealt with as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, to confirm that this would be something unusual, as you described it in your last answer, in this situation if the Chief of Staff has an opportunity to speak to his corps commander, would you expect him to report and discuss the matters with his corps commander and either to try to get the additional tasking modified or cancelled or at least to get more resources to do it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that in such situations it is necessary for an officer to obtain additional information, this didn't in itself mean that this officer should talk to the corps commander or his deputy, since additional information can be obtained from another relevant officer within the corps depending on the unit in question, depending on the requirements and depending on the activities or the type of activity being required of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But just to add on, if he does have the opportunity to speak to the corps commander, is that something you would expect the Chief of Staff to discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I think he has already answered the question at least a couple of different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we don't seem to be in agreement with you in the first place. So let's proceed with the answer -- by majority, by majority. I agree with Judge Kwon on this. Yes, General, if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Always when a subordinate officer has an opportunity of talking to the commander, it is quite normal for him to check everything with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'll move to my next question. Always again in the same situation having been informed about this additional tasking, the Chief of Staff must suddenly leave the brigade command to accomplish other duties. Would you expect before leaving the brigade command that the Chief of Staff would at least ensure that one member of the brigade is fully informed of the ongoing situation concerning this additional tasking imposed on the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. When any officer is leaving and the most senior officer who will stand in for him is there, he is duty-bound to create such conditions in which the officer who will stand in for him has all the information about the situation in the unit that will enable him to reach an appropriate decision in view of the commander's wishes and goals. Otherwise, the officer standing in will not be able to make an appropriate decision in an emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, I move to my next question. Suppose that is in the same situation the return of the brigade commander is announced two days later at a time when the situation in the brigade has become even more critical because the brigade is involved at the same time in combat activities as well as in the additional tasking which was imposed on it. My question is the following: Would you expect the Chief of Staff, if he is present at the brigade command, when the commander returns to prepare and give him a full briefing as soon as he arrives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I must comment either on the question or the interpretation. It says here, "if a brigade is involved in combat activities," a brigade cannot be involved in combat activities, it carries out combat activities. So we have to be precise. The moment the senior or the commanding officer returns, the officer who had been standing in for him and deputising for him is duty-bound to brief the returning senior officer in great detail about the situation in the unit and all the problems and issues that have arisen. This is clearly defined but the commanding officer when he returns can delay this if he has other urgent obligations, and only ask to be informed of the most salient points, the crucial points.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You went directly into my next question, General, and that is in addition to the fact that the officer who was standing in as a duty to prepare such a report, would the brigade commander returning expect to be fully briefed about everything in the brigade when he returns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in this circumstance he has clearly answered the question. If you look at the previous answer, he actually expands on the question and says that the brigade commander can delay it or not delay it. So in terms of expectation, I think that this question is inappropriate to put to this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, or do you wish to move on to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can move along, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of moving to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In terms, General, for the brigade commander to obtain that full briefing, one way he could obtain the information about the brigade would be to consult with the brigade duty officer. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer can only inform him about the current situation and the ongoing activities of the brigade. For him to get a complete overview, he has to be informed by the person who had stood in for him or deputised for him in the presence of his other assistants and deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in exactly this scenario which you describe a little earlier, and that is that because of time constraints, the commander is not able to get the full briefing, would you expect him to arrange a meeting with his Chief of Staff at the earliest opportunity in order to get that briefing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely so. He would initially be asked to be informed of the most important facts, and then he would say, You will give me more detailed information at such and such a time or after such and such a thing takes place. So he would tell him when he expected the full briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In my next question, upon returning to his brigade, suppose the commander was ordered for the brigade to carry out combat activities immediately with the aim of blocking an armed enemy force which has entered into his area of operations. Would you expect the commander to request, as part of the full briefing, an update on the use and availability of his engineering resources?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sort of situation you have described, if along with the other forces that are necessary for the commander to carry out the task, he also needed engineer units or forces, he would ask for information about that. If they were not indispensable for the carrying out of the task, his question would be to be told what were the forces available and what was the situation there that he could use for the task ahead of him, and he would not seek any other information at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, based on your extensive military experience, carrying out combat activities with the aim of blocking an enemy force, is that likely to require the use of engineering resources?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two types of blocking, as you say, of an enemy force. For one type of blocking engineering resources are not needed and for the other type they are needed. Any blocking that makes it possible to take up positions in time and put those positions in order would require engineering resources, but the type of blocking that does not provide for sufficient time for engineering works at the positions only combat units are used which block units within part of their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I now move to my last question, General. And this refers to your testimony during your examination-in-chief at page 30008 at lines 23 to 25 you said: "The operative duty officer is subordinated to the commander." And at page 30022, lines 8 to 13, you were talking about the command post of a unit as being composed of several elements, and you stated the following: "There is a single command post which is composed of several elements. One of the elements of a command post is the basic command post. Another element is the forward command post. Therefore, a command post is a system made of a number of other systems and subsystems, so wherever you are, either in one of the systems or subsystems, you are within the system itself." Do you recall your testimony to that effect, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And also the context in which I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following: When a brigade commander is exercising his command over his brigade at the brigade forward command post, in your opinion is he still responsible for the ongoing activities at the command post in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the commander of the brigade is at the forward command post, he is still the brigade commander and is responsible for his brigade. Where he is has no effect on his responsibility for his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just one quick follow-on question to that. Would the duty operations -- the brigade duty operations officer at the brigade command, is he operating under the authority of the brigade commander even though his brigade commander is at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mentioned some important elements, that is that the operations duty officer is immediately subordinate to the commander and the most senior duty officer in the unit, and that in itself contains my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we will not cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. General, my name is Dragan Krgovic and on behalf of the Defence of General Gvero I will put some questions to you connected to your testimony here. I have to stoop down because of the position of this microphone, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, testifying on the 14th of January of this year, and that's on transcript page 30088 for the sake of my colleagues, you spoke about a meeting held in President Karadzic's office on the 16th of March, 1995, which was attended by some officers. Do you remember talking about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I remember that I was interrupted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You then mentioned that apart from President Karadzic and according to the visitors book maintained by Mr. Karadzic's secretary, Generals Subotic, who at the time was the military advisor of the president of the republic, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General Manojlo Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff, VRS; General Tolimir, the chief of security; and General Djukic, the assistant for logistics. I do apologise, General Tolimir, the chief of -- or the assistant for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to know if my colleague could give us a reference. It was not on the 14th of January and we don't have the correct page. I do not believe that General Djukic was mentioned during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember myself, but Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On 14th of January, page 30088 [as interpreted] according to the copy of the transcript I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want time to check, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just not sure if General Djukic was mentioned or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 83, last two digit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the previous page. It begins on the previous page, and the reply which was interrupted ends on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From line 9 on page 30083 and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are right, Judge Kwon. We can go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that these were the participants and that at that meeting when referring to officers and their responsibilities, that the persons attending that meeting were all persons who were necessary for a document such as Directive number 7 of the Supreme Command being prepared. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that the persons were essential, not all of them perhaps, but that they were essential or important for this document to be drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were they indispensable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the participation of the assistants for morale, religious affairs, and so on was not indispensable for this directive to be drawn up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to confirm this, I would be disparaging a very important sector. I can conclude the following: Bearing in mind the events that took place and the details in the diary or log-book, at that point conversations were held with every person who was essential for the drawing up of such a document. And if there had been more people that would not have been amiss, but these were the truly indispensable ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, please allow a short pause. Try to avoid overlapping now that you are speaking the same language, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The portion that could be provided by the assistant for morale would not be essential for this directive of the Supreme Command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just that portion. One could leave out from the directive other elements too. You can see that there are many elements there that are not contained in every directive. It's well known that a directive can be issued on only one page with only one task. Whoever issues the directive always evaluates what the scope of this directive should be which he wishes to pass on to his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he's the one who decides who to involve in the work regarding the elaboration of the directive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He decides who he will consult before he reaches a final decision concerning the directive. It's up to him alone to decide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, you spoke in your testimony and you mentioned this also in part in your report that Directive number 7 differs from the other directives you have had occasion to see. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this directive in the form in which it was finally signed is a state document containing illogical and imprecise portions, do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P5. Could the witness please be shown page 10 in the B/C/S version and page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have page 10 before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an empty screen. Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the lower part beginning with number 6 be enlarged for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the part numbered 6 is support for combat operations, and in point 6.1 we have moral and psychological support. It would be normal for this to be followed by 6.2 or 6.3, other kinds of support if we have 6.1 here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says here 6.1, from the aspect of methodology, it would be normal to expect to have at least one other element of support. We know that usually there are seven such elements, but here it would be normal to expect for at least one other element to be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to the next page, please. That's page -- it's the same page in English but the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at this page we don't have 6.2 or 6.3, nothing left in terms of security, right? Or support, right, you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to the previous page, page number 10. Number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please read the last sentence which cites, "by planning, organising, and coordinated information and propaganda action by the state leaders," and then on to the next page of this directive, please. The previous sentence does not continue here, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly one can see that this is not the continuation of the previous portion of the sentence and the entire chapter in relation to support for combat operations was produced in an entirely unsoldierly manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you analyse the portion right here, you can see these elements being introduced such as logistics, PVO support, things to do with mobilisation. This entire paragraph does not contain anything, at least in my view, that would corresponds with morale and psychological support. Not something that would seem to be in keeping with the rules of the military profession; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only does it not corresponds with this element of support for combat operation, this entire paragraph is not in keeping with its purpose. This entire paragraph that relates to support for combat operations and then with a specific emphasis on 6.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this seems to confirm what you said in chief. This portion was not produced by a qualified military person. In terms of style it would seem to reflect more of a political background or a state background rather than a military one; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, anything but military. This directive is not a military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And especially this particular portion; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are others. I do not want to be -- seem to be introducing some sort of hierarchy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 5D759.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is your expert report. Let me pick up what you said about non-military terminology. There are other portions of this directive that are not military like or soldierly but would rather seem to indicate some sort of political background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have paragraph 139 shown on our screens. The page number is 53. I'm talking about your expert report. The Serbian reference is 53. The English would be 65, page 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
